title: Stage 4: Undo and Redo
summary: A generic higher-order reducer that adds history to any reducer.

steps.title: History as state
body: Undo is easy once state is immutable: keep the **old states**.
redo ▶  past: [s0, s1]   present: s2   future: []
new change ▶  past: [s0, s1, s2]   present: s3   future: []   (future is discarded)
Because unchanged parts are shared between states (stage 2), keeping 50 states costs little memory.

You will write `undoable(reducer)`: a **higher-order reducer** that takes any reducer and returns a new one over `History<S>`. It is generic, so it works for the board and for anything else, and `boardReducer` does not change at all.

code: let past: number[] = [1, 2], present = 3, future: number[] = [];
steps.explain: The first assignment is an undo, the second a redo. Destructuring assignment evaluates the whole right side first.

steps.prompt: Why must a no-op action (the reducer returned the same state) leave the history unchanged?
options: Otherwise pressing undo would appear to do nothing, because it would step back to an identical state
Because `past` can hold only distinct numbers

steps.title: undoable
prompt: interface History<S> { past: S[]; present: S; future: S[] }
function undoable<S, A extends { type: string }>(reducer: (state: S, action: A) => S, limit = 50)
- `undo`: move `present` to the front of `future` and the last of `past` to `present`; with an empty `past` return the same history
- `redo`: the reverse; with an empty `future` return the same history

- any other action: run `reducer`; if it returns the same state, return the same history; otherwise push the old present onto `past` (keeping at most `limit` entries, dropping the oldest), set the new present, and clear `future`
